soil-bio-040.q: How do earthworms breathe, given that they have no special respiratory organs?

soil-bio-041.q: Which ecological group of earthworms builds deep vertical burrows and pulls leaves down into mineral soil?
soil-bio-041.a: Anecic worms, such as Lumbricus terrestris, which come up from permanent vertical burrows to gather leaves.

soil-bio-075.q: Which two groups of microbes produce geosmin?
soil-bio-075.a: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, and actinomycetes, mainly Streptomyces.

soil-bio-043.q: What can invading earthworms do to the banded profile of a podzol?
soil-bio-043.a: They can erase it, mixing the organic, E and upper B horizons into a single dark Ap horizon.

soil-bio-070.q: Which bacterium is the most commonly applied microbial inoculant, and what does it do?
soil-bio-070.a: Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.

soil-bio-009.q: Why do soil microbes respire less as salinity rises?
soil-bio-009.a: Because they have less available water.

soil-bio-085.q: If springtails do not decompose organic matter directly, how do they speed decomposition?
soil-bio-085.a: By fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbial communities.

soil-bio-016.q: How does a lysogenic phage differ from a lytic one?
soil-bio-016.a: A lytic phage kills its host to release virions; a lysogenic phage joins the host genome.

soil-bio-081.q: What largely sets the stature of tropical montane elfin forests?

soil-bio-036.q: What is the difference between basal and substrate-induced respiration?
soil-bio-036.a: Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars.

soil-bio-066.q: How far below the sea floor have mineral-forming microorganisms been found?

soil-bio-010.q: Why is the diversity of soil life hard to measure?
soil-bio-010.a: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed.

soil-bio-032.q: Why can isopods die if kept from eating their own faeces?
soil-bio-032.a: On nutrient-poor litter, the microbes colonising their pellets enrich the food.

soil-bio-027.q: Which energy channels carry the largest flow in soil flow webs?
soil-bio-027.a: The bacterial and fungal channels; the root-herbivory channel carries much less.

soil-bio-062.q: On the sandplains of southern Western Australia, what do most plants rely on to get phosphorus and sulfur?

soil-bio-193.q: True or false: nematodes decompose organic matter.
soil-bio-193.a: False: they feed on living material, regulating bacterial numbers and community composition.

soil-bio-088.q: Why do copiotrophs lose out to oligotrophs once nutrients run out?
soil-bio-088.a: They live a feast-and-famine life, using nutrients fast but surviving poorly when supplies run out.

soil-bio-068.q: Why is biocementation unsuited to soils rich in fines?
soil-bio-068.a: Bacteria cannot pass pore throats smaller than about 0.4 μm.

soil-bio-080.q: How can extracellular polymeric substances lower a soil's hydraulic conductivity?
soil-bio-080.a: Together with microbial cells they block soil pores, a process called bioclogging.

soil-bio-139.q: Name a crop whose taproot serves as a storage organ.
soil-bio-139.a: Carrot, radish or turnip: many taproots are storage organs.

soil-bio-135.q: Why do most roots of most plants lie fairly close to the surface?
soil-bio-135.a: Nutrients are more available and aeration is better there.

soil-bio-198.q: What happens to a root's growth if its cap is removed?
soil-bio-198.a: It grows at random, because statoliths in the cap's statocytes drive gravitropism.

soil-bio-149.q: Compared with the rhizosphere, are microbes in bulk soil more varied or more abundant?
soil-bio-149.a: More varied; they are more abundant in the rhizosphere.

soil-bio-173.q: What does an ectomycorrhizal fungus supply its host in return for food?
soil-bio-173.a: Nitrogen: it gets about 15% of the host's food and supplies up to 86% of its nitrogen needs.

soil-bio-202.q: When can a non-systemic endophyte turn pathogenic?

soil-bio-168.q: How does tillage reduce a crop's phosphorus supply from arbuscular fungi?
soil-bio-168.a: It breaks up soil macrostructure and the hyphal network, leaving the network non-infective.

soil-bio-192.q: When do microbes switch on siderophore production?

soil-bio-145.q: Why can strigolactones released by roots backfire on a plant?
soil-bio-145.a: The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects them.

soil-bio-185.q: What is traded across the Hartig net?
soil-bio-185.a: Nutrients from the fungus's outer mycelium pass into the root's apoplast, and plant sugars pass back to feed the fungus.

soil-bio-169.q: For restoring desertified land, which worked best: a native fungal mixture, a single exotic species or no inoculum?
soil-bio-169.a: The mixture of native arbuscular fungi, which improved soil quality more over the long term.

soil-bio-200.q: Which enzyme lets Frankia turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia?

soil-bio-189.q: What can happen to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi under high nitrogen?

soil-bio-190.q: Which two symbioses use the common symbiosis signalling pathway?
soil-bio-190.a: Arbuscular mycorrhiza, its ancestral user, and the younger root-nodule symbiosis with rhizobia.

soil-bio-106.q: What separates the L, F and H litter layers?
soil-bio-106.a: How decomposed they are: L is little decomposed, F partly and H fully.
